messages.content: Maintain a 2:1 ratio of declarative to interrogative sentences in your response. Show a metric space (M, d) is complete if and only if any sequence (F_n) of nonempty closed subsets of M with - F_{n+1} \subset F_n - diam F_n \rightarrow 0 as n \rightarrow \infty has a nonempty intersection

message.content:
In the forward direction, M is complete, (F_n) is a sequence of nonempty closed sets with F_{n+1} \subset F_n and diameters tending to zero, and x_n is chosen from F_n.
Why is (x_n) Cauchy?
For m>n, x_m and x_n both lie in F_n, so d(x_m,x_n) \le diam F_n, which tends to zero.
Completeness gives x in M, and closedness gives x in every F_n, so the intersection is nonempty.
How does the reverse direction work?
In the reverse direction, (x_n) is an arbitrary Cauchy sequence, and the hypothesis says that every sequence of nonempty closed sets with F_{n+1} \subset F_n and diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection.
Which closed sets apply to (x_n)?
For (x_n), we define F_n as the closure of the tail {x_m : m \ge n}; these sets are nonempty, closed, nested, and have vanishing diameter because (x_n) is Cauchy.
The intersection contains some x, and d(x_n,x) \le diam F_n forces convergence, so M is complete.

Since diam closure A = diam A (in metric spaces). So F_n = closure({x_m:m>=n}) are nonempty closed, nested, diam F_n ->0. By hypothesis, intersection nonempty. Pick x in intersection. Then for any epsilon, pick n with diam F_n<epsilon. Since x in F_n, and x_n in F_n, d(x_n,x)<diam F_n<epsilon for all n? Wait if x in intersection, x in F_k for all k.
